clinicalPearls: A congenital cochleovestibular malformation in which the cochlea has fewer than the normal turns with a deficient interscalar septum at the apex
In the classic incomplete partition type II it is often accompanied by a dilated vestibule and an enlarged vestibular aqueduct
Hearing loss is sensorineural or mixed and may be stable, fluctuating, or progressive
There is an increased risk of recurrent meningitis and cerebrospinal-fluid leak because of an abnormal communication with the subarachnoid space
It is frequently associated with SLC26A4 variants and overlaps clinically with Pendred syndrome
Imaging is essential both to make the diagnosis and to anticipate a perilymph or cerebrospinal-fluid gusher at surgery
Cochlear implantation is often feasible and effective with appropriate surgical planning
reference.pathophysiology: Mondini dysplasia arises from arrested cochlear development during embryogenesis, leaving a cochlea with incomplete coiling and a deficient modiolus and interscalar septum, most typically the incomplete partition type II pattern combined with a dilated vestibule and enlarged vestibular aqueduct. The malformed and often incompletely separated fluid compartments impair normal cochlear mechanics and endolymph homeostasis, producing sensorineural or mixed hearing loss. A deficient bony partition can create an abnormal communication with the cerebrospinal fluid, predisposing to fluid gusher during surgery and to recurrent meningitis, and many cases share the SLC26A4-related mechanism seen in Pendred syndrome and isolated enlarged vestibular aqueduct.
additionalDifferentials: Enlarged vestibular aqueduct without cochlear partition defect
Incomplete partition types I and III
Common cavity and other cochlear aplasia or hypoplasia
Acquired sensorineural hearing loss with normal anatomy
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution temporal bone imaging to define cochlear turns and the interscalar septum
Magnetic resonance imaging to assess membranous structures and the cochlear nerve
Pure-tone audiometry to characterise the type and progression of loss
SLC26A4 genetic testing and assessment for Pendred features
Thyroid evaluation when Pendred syndrome is suspected
Vestibular testing when balance symptoms are present
redFlags: Recurrent meningitis or cerebrospinal-fluid rhinorrhoea indicating an abnormal fluid communication
Radiological features predicting a gusher at implantation
Coexisting thyroid or systemic features suggesting a syndrome
reference.prognosis: Hearing outcomes vary with the severity of the malformation, but with careful surgical planning cochlear implantation generally provides good rehabilitation, while the meningitis risk warrants vaccination and prompt treatment of leaks.
pitfalls: Missing the malformation by not obtaining dedicated temporal bone imaging
Overlooking recurrent meningitis as a marker of an inner-ear fluid communication
Failing to anticipate a gusher during cochlear implantation
Not investigating for coexisting Pendred syndrome
references: Sennaroglu Classification of Inner Ear Malformations
management: Auditory rehabilitation tailored to severity, with hearing aids for milder loss and cochlear implantation for severe-to-profound loss, planning surgery to anticipate and control a perilymph or cerebrospinal-fluid gusher
Pneumococcal and other indicated vaccination to reduce the risk of recurrent meningitis
Prompt surgical repair of any cerebrospinal-fluid leak and urgent antimicrobial treatment of meningitis
Serial pure-tone audiometry to monitor fluctuating or progressive loss, with counselling to avoid head trauma and barotrauma
SLC26A4 genetic testing and thyroid assessment where Pendred syndrome features are present
Multidisciplinary otology and audiovestibular care with speech and language therapy for communication development
Genetic counselling and family screening where an SLC26A4-related mechanism is identified
